To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the HAff1 domain sequence of hemagglutanin of clinical H1n1 influenza viruses, associated with chronic respiratory problems in pigs of Quebec, was studied.
the H1N1 viruses associated with chronic and acute respiratory problems in pigs are antigenically and genetically different.

the H1 hemagglutin of the SwQc91, associated with acute and SwQc81 strains, associated with chronic respiratory influenza, were distinct from the hemagglutin from the SwQc329 and SwQc174 strains, associated with acute disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic and antigenic characterization of hemagglu- tinins from H1N1 viruses associated with acute respiratory disease and chronic respiratory disease in Quebec.
the genetic and antigenic characterization of hemaggluttinin of H1N1 swine influenza viruses isolated from pigs with acute or chronic respiratory diseases.
the genetic analysis of H1N1 viruses associated with respiratory diseases in pigs in order to identify genetic determinants of virulence and to develop new vaccines against these viruses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the H1N1 virus associated with chronic disease in swine in Quebec, are closely related to the classical A/SwQc91 virus, but differ in their antigenic sites, and therefore, are not antigenically related.
the SwQc91 strain is antigenically different from other classical H1N1 strains, such as SwQc81, SwQc1746 and SwQc1196.
the SwQc91, SwQc329l and SwQc1741 viruses were antigenically related and were genetically distinct from SwQcl92 virus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the hemagglutin of the H1N1 swine influenza viruses associated with chronic respiratory diseases were antigenically related, whereas the hemagglutins of H1N1 viruses associated with acute respiratory diseases were antigenic distinct.

the H1N1 virus associated with chronic disease in Quebec is antigenically and genotypically distinct from the classical H1N1 strain, but closely related to other H1N1 viruses associated with chronic respiratory problems in pigs.
the H1N1 strains isolated in Quebec during recent outbreaks were antigenically related and were genetically distant from the classical SwQc81 virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no evidence of a direct association of the hemagglutini of the H1N1 swine influenza virus with the development of chronic respiratory diseases in the pig.

the hemagglutination domain of HA of the clinical H1N11 influenza viruses, associated with chronic respiratory problems in pigs, showed considerable variation in comparison with the classical A/Sw/Qc81 strain.
the hemagglutins of H1N1 swine influenza viruses associated with acute or chronic respiratory disease in pigs are genetically distinct.
